data.title: Lululemon Appoints Two Key Executives Amid Leadership Shakeup
data.description:
By Natalie Weger

Lululemon Athletica appointed two new key executives as Chief Executive Heidi O'Neill rounds out her leadership team to help address slumping sales at the athleisure company.

The company on Friday said it has appointed Ben Hallam as chief brand officer and Emily Sunderland as chief strategy officer, effective Nov. 9 and Nov. 23, respectively

Hallam, who succeeds Nikki Neuburger, most recently served as the senior vice president of marketing at Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts.

Sunderland was a managing director and partner at Boston Consulting Group, succeeding Rachel Acheson.

O'Neill, a former Nike executive, has already made several executive changes since she took the helm of the company in September. Last month, she brought on the former head of Gap's Athleta brand as president and chief product officer, and also tapped a former Walmart executive as chief operating officer.

Lululemon said it's still looking for a chief technology officer and chief communications officer.

Write to Natalie Weger at natalie.weger@wsj.com.

data.title: IPOs Struggle in Tech Selloff. Berkshire Has a Winner. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Andrew Bary

The old investment adage to avoid initial public offerings has held up this year, as many stocks are trading well below their IPO prices.

Barron's looked at 18 companies that made their U.S. stock-market debuts in 2026, including marquee offerings like SpaceX, Cerebras Systems, Innio, Madison Air Solutions and Jersey Mike's, found that 15 of them are below their offering prices. Many are down 50% or more.

SK Hynix, already public in South Korea, made its U.S. debut in July through an offering of American depositary shares. That stock also is trading below its U.S. offering price in July.

Why do IPOs often falter? Companies that come public often are in hot industries, and carry high valuations to reflect investor optimism. That enthusiasm often wanes, however. This year, some deals were keyed off the AI buildout and enthusiasm for that trend has faded.

There are some winners, notably Arxis, a defense contractor with an aerospace focus; Pershing Square, Bill Ackman's investment management company, and Bending Spoons, the rollup of mature tech companies like AOL.

Give Berkshire Hathaway some credit. The company headed now by CEO Greg Abel picked the right deal when it invested $600 million in Bending Spoons at the July IPO at $29 a share. The stock traded recently at $45, up 55%. In October, Berkshire bought another $330 million of stock at $33.

Berkshire rarely buys IPOs — reflecting former CEO Warren Buffett's well-founded aversion to them. It participated in Snowflake's IPO in 2020.

Looking at some of the larger deals, SpaceX trades around $131, against an IPO price of $135; Cerebras at $82, less than half its IPO price of $185; and SK Hynix at $124, versus its U.S. offering price of $149.

One of the better ways to play IPOs in a diversified way is through the Renaissance IPO ETF. It adds newly public companies every three months as part of a regular rebalancing and companies cycle out after three years. Individual holdings are capped at a 10% weighting at rebalancing.

Its largest holdings now are SpaceX at nearly 10%, followed by SK Hynix and Astera Labs, both at more than 7%. The ETF, now around $45, is off about 2% so far this year.

Be careful about SK Hynix ADRs. While chip stocks have come under pressure, SK Hynix's U.S. shares trade at a big premium to the Korean shares that Barron's estimates is close to 50%.

Busted IPOs also can be a good place to look for values, and there are many companies to comb through this year.

Write to Andrew Bary at andrew.bary@barrons.com

data.title: Nasdaq rebounds but posts fourth straight weekly decline
data.description:
Key points:
  • Indexes: Dow slips, Nasdaq, S&P gain
  • Tech stocks bounce back from worst day in more than a year
  • October jobs report surprises to the upside

By Colin Barr and Shashwat Chauhan

Technology stocks bounced back on Friday from their worst drubbing in more than a year, but the Nasdaq Composite Index posted a fourth consecutive weekly decline as investors sifted for clues about what comes next in the AI trade.

Gains within technology were broadly shared, with the semiconductor index rallying 4.2%. Nvidia rose 2.8%, Advanced Micro Devices added 11% and Sandisk rebounded almost 4%. Shares within the sector opened strongly and held much of their gains, with the Nasdaq ending up 1.1% after trading as much as 2% higher.

The broad revival underscores investor faith in the AI buildout that has driven US stock indexes to dozens of record closes this year, despite a shakeout that began with a US long-term Treasury yield spike in August and the stock volatility of the past month.

“We still think AI is the dominant theme in this bull market,” said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services in Atlanta. “We are still giving technology the benefit of the doubt.”

The S&P 500 climbed 23 points, or 0.32%, to end the session at 7,376.86 points. The Nasdaq gained 264 points to 24,579.43 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 237 points, or 0.46%, to 51,285.73 points.

Lerner said he views the selloff this week, which has taken the Nasdaq into correction territory denoting a 10% decline from its peak a month ago, as likely offering a longer-term buying opportunity for many investors. For the week, the Nasdaq declined 3.4%, the S&P dropped 2.7% and the Dow slipped 0.9%.

“AI has gone on trial several times in this cycle and come away with an innocent verdict,” said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for LPL Financial in Charlotte, North Carolina. Referring to the US midterm election results that spurred heavy selling in AI stocks, he said, “This week we saw a little bit of a knee-jerk reaction.”

The S&P 500 sectors were mixed, with information technology leading gains and consumer staples and healthcare lagging. The benchmark index had its worst week in more than a year.

US nonfarm payrolls increased more than expected in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, suggesting the labor market remained resilient. Traders added to bets that the Federal Reserve could hike rates as soon as next month, with a 78% chance of a December move compared with a 70% chance seen earlier, according to LSEG.

"Those are strong numbers,” said Joe Saluzzi, co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading in Chatham, New Jersey. But he asked, “Will the Fed want to raise interest rates in the face of a market which is teetering?"

Tesla rose 4.2% and SpaceX jumped 8.6% among technology shares bouncing back from Thursday’s plunge. Among other stock movers, software firm Atlassian dropped 16% after reporting first-quarter results. Airbnb climbed 12% after the vacation rental platform raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast.

Oil prices were slightly lower, adding to bullish sentiment for riskier assets, and were on track for sharp weekly declines. The S&P 500 energy index dropped 12% for the week, its worst performance since April 2025.

Despite the volatility, Turnquist said a bullish sign for the AI buildout is the performance of copper, a major ingredient in data centers and other technology. Copper futures remain above their 200-day moving average and their September lows, he said.

“If this is real demand destruction on AI, you’d think copper would start to roll over,” Turnquist said. “It’s not a perfect barometer, but I look at it as a reality check.”

data.title: Hawaiian Electric Profit, Sales Rise After American Savings Bank Sale
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton

Hawaiian Electric Industries logged higher profit and revenue in the third quarter, thanks in large part to selling a portion of its stake in American Savings Bank.

The utilities company posted a profit of $35 million, or 20 cents a share, compared with $31 million, or 18 cents a share, a year earlier.

Stripping out certain one-time items, such as those related to the Maui wildfire, adjusted per-share earnings were 13 cents a share.

Revenue rose 28% to $1.01 billion.

Hawaiian Electric's holding and other companies, which includes non-utility businesses, swung to a profit of $22 million, from a loss of $6 million. That primarily reflected pre-tax gains on the sale of American Savings Bank shares.

Hawaiian Electric sold 35% of its 9.9% stake in the bank's initial public offering, which was in September. Its remaining stake is about 6.4%.

Within the company's core business profit fell to $13 million from $37 million, mainly due to higher costs.

Operations and management expenses were higher than the year before, mostly due to storm costs in August and September.

data.title: Robust Hiring Defied Expectations in October, With 165,000 New Jobs — WSJ
data.description:
By Justin Lahart

The U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October, in a sign that the labor market could be strengthening.

The numbers

Friday's report from the Labor Department topped economists' expectations for a 59,000 job gain. The unemployment rate, meanwhile, slipped to 4.1%, lower than expectations for 4.2%.

Jobs figures for both September and August were revised higher by a combined 84,000. That is a strong indication that the job market has pulled out of its midyear doldrums. The economy has added an average of 137,000 jobs a month over the past three months.

"It's as good as can be, really," said Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon.

Daco said that the drop in the unemployment rate was especially notable given that the labor-force participation rate — the share of the working-age population either working or looking for work — picked up last month. That is an indication that more people were entering the labor market and finding jobs.

Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo, pointed out that the unemployment rate has now been under 5% for roughly five years. That puts it just short of a record 64-month stretch from 1965 to 1970.

Where jobs were gained and lost

October's employment growth was driven by an increase of 70,000 professional and business-services jobs — well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the previous 12 months.

That could be a sign that artificial intelligence isn't yet sapping white-collar jobs to the degree some people fear.

The finance sector — one area seen as heavily exposed to AI — added 7,000 jobs, but has been in a weakening trend. And the information sector shed 1,000 jobs.

Elsewhere, the AI build-out has for some time been fueling jobs for workers who are building data centers.

Construction overall shed 3,000 jobs. On a more granular level, however, the report showed that employers last month hired almost 8,000 nonresidential specialty-trade contractors, workers such as electricians who are in high demand at data-center sites.

At the same time, employers shed more than 15,000 such residential roles, a sign of how higher interest rates are slowing housing construction.

Manufacturing added 19,000 jobs, bolstered by gains in computer and electronic-product machinery and primary metal manufacturing. All of those sectors are seen as beneficiaries of the AI build-out.

What AI means for the jobs market

On balance, Samuel Tombs, chief U.S. economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, reckons that gains from AI in areas like manufacturing aren't enough to completely offset losses elsewhere.

"I think AI is a modest drag, but it is not a dramatically deteriorating picture," he said.

Healthcare was a continued source of employment growth, adding 42,000 jobs.

Tombs also thinks that the renewed strength in the jobs report in part reflects what has been a strong stock market — Thursday's meltdown aside — and a relatively easy financing environment for companies. The volatility that financial markets have recently experienced could change that.

Wages

Average hourly earnings were up 3.1% from a year earlier. That likely marked the seventh month in a row where earnings growth fell short of inflation.

But from a month earlier, hourly earnings were up a robust 0.4%. That was in part from the broadening in job growth into areas with better pay, such as professional and business services.

How markets reacted

Stocks rose following the report, taking back some of the ground they lost in Thursday's sharp, AI-driven selloff. Treasury yields were little changed, however, while futures markets continued to signal an expectation that Federal Reserve policymakers will likely raise rates when they next meet in December.

What this means for the Fed

Fed policymakers right now are more focused on inflation, which has remained firmly above their 2% target, than on the job market, which has remained sturdy despite some weakness earlier this year.

Officials will have one additional month of jobs data to parse by the time they gather for their next meeting. They will also be watching closely to see if this week's market turmoil turns into a sustained selloff. That means that Friday's jobs numbers could become just a footnote by the time they gather in December.

Midterm postmortem

Dissatisfaction with the job market — and the economy overall — might have been a factor in Democrats' victory over Republicans in this week's midterm elections.

One reason is that wages have struggled to keep up with inflation. That means that, even as the economy has powered ahead, a smaller and smaller share of economic growth has gone directly to workers. On Thursday, the Labor Department reported that the share of nonfarm business output accruing to workers' compensation fell to 53% in the third quarter — the lowest level in 80 years of data.

Another issue is that while layoffs have been low, so has the pace of hiring. That has made it difficult for people trying to break into the job market, such as new graduates. The low-hire market has also made it harder for people to switch jobs — one of the main ways for workers to get pay jumps.

data.title: UC Automotive, Used Vehicle Retail and Automotive Services, Files for Nasdaq Capital Market IPO
data.description:
UC Automotive Holdings Inc. filed a Form F-1 registration statement for a proposed initial public offering of its common shares. The company has applied to list on the Nasdaq Capital Market, but the share count and price range have not been disclosed. Based in British Columbia, UC Automotive sells used vehicles and provides leasing, rental, financing support and related automotive services.

Business Description

UC Automotive operates a used vehicle dealership and automotive services business focused on Greater Vancouver. Through its Canadian subsidiaries, it sells used vehicles to consumers and also sources and wholesales vehicles, provides short-term rentals and longer-term leasing and rent-to-own programs, assists customers with financing, and coordinates after-sales services. Vehicle sales are its primary revenue source.

Market Overview

  • Total addressable market: Frost & Sullivan estimates the Canadian used vehicle trading and services market at US$100.0 billion in 2025.
  • Market growth: The Canadian market grew at a 7.8% CAGR from 2021 to 2025 and is projected to reach US$136.3 billion by 2030, a projected 6.4% CAGR from 2026.
  • Market position: Frost & Sullivan places UC Auto in the second tier of Canadian independent used vehicle dealers by 2025 revenue; the company reported approximately C$52.3 million in revenue.
  • Key competitors: Clutch, HGrégoire, AutoCanada, Auto Outlet, Car-On, Canada Drives, AutoPark, DriveNation, Need A Car and Cardora.
  • Industry trends: The market is shifting toward online-to-offline sales, full-lifecycle services, digital operations and selective AI adoption in vehicle sourcing, pricing and inventory management.

Operational Metrics

  • Customers: As of June 30, 2026, the company had 20 active short-term rental customers and five active long-term rent-to-own customers.
  • Locations: As of June 30, 2026, it operated one retail location, one service shop and one parking lot, all in Richmond, British Columbia.
  • Geographic presence: Operations are concentrated in Greater Vancouver, Canada.
  • Partnerships: The company had commercial referral arrangements with 11 third-party banks or financial institutions as of June 30, 2026.
  • Vehicle transactions: The company sold 1,090 vehicles in the six months ended June 30, 2026, compared with 990 in the same period of 2025; it sold 1,128 vehicles in 2025.
  • Financing activity: From April 21, 2016 through June 30, 2026, the company facilitated 304 financing transactions through third parties and originated 46, for 350 total transactions.
  • Fleet and staff: The leasing and rental fleet included 13 vehicles; the company had 23 sales consultants and seven customer service personnel as of June 30, 2026.
  • Vehicle acquisition leads: Carkuku generated 207 visible acquisition leads during a campaign period from April 11 to May 11, 2026; more recently, lead volume averaged approximately two per day.

Financials Highlights

  • Revenue (current): US$22,134,359 for the six months ended June 30, 2026; US$37,469,259 for 2025.
  • Revenue growth: Six-month revenue declined 1.4% year over year; full-year revenue declined 10.6% in 2025.
  • Gross profit: US$1,837,089 for the six months ended June 30, 2026 (8.3% margin).
  • Operating income: US$256,154 for the six months ended June 30, 2026.
  • Net income: US$218,805 for the six months ended June 30, 2026.

IPO Structure

  • Issuer: UC Automotive Holdings Inc.
  • Filing date: November 06, 2026
  • Exchange: Nasdaq Capital Market
  • Lead underwriters: Kingswood Capital Partners, LLC
  • Use of proceeds: Approximately 40% for vehicle inventory and working capital, 30% for retail and rental expansion, 20% for technology and digital infrastructure, and 10% for general corporate and working capital purposes.

data.title: Data centers run on debt. That was a problem for bonds this year - and it's only going to get worse.
data.description:
By Joy Wiltermuth

AI debt issuance this year overwhelmed investor portfolios, and has disappointed from a performance perspective. The funding need won't get any better with Democrats in control of Congress.

The AI buildout was on the ballot in the midterm elections. The funding blitz on Wall Street could slow, but isn't likely to stop.

The copious amounts of debt rolling out to finance the artificial-intelligence buildout has rattled the bond market this year, as borrowers have needed to pay higher interest rates to find takers for all the supply.

Don't expect the midterm election results to change that. As Democrats take control of Congress in January, some on Wall Street think any slowdown in the building of data centers could reduce the need for AI builders to borrow. That could reduce bond supply, and provide some relief to bonds now underwater in portfolios.

Less supply could boost the appeal of all those existing AI bonds, and their prices. But a recent report from Goldman Sachs says not to count on a smaller borrowing need.

AI debt issuance this year smashed Wall Street's supply expectations, swamped investor portfolios and disappointed from a performance perspective.

With Meta Platforms (META), Microsoft (MSFT), Oracle (ORCL) and others borrowing another $67 billion since late October, Goldman Sachs's credit strategy team tallied AI "hyperscaler" debt supply at $296 billion already this year, in a Thursday report. That was well above the bank's $250 billion forecast for 2026.

Another $440 billion in hyperscaler debt supply is now expected in 2027, albeit with access to capital markets "to be somewhat uneven across issuers and highly dependent on the market tone," the Goldman team, led Amanda Lynam, wrote in the report.

Angst around AI caught up with tech stocks after Tuesday's midterm elections swept Democrats to power - not just in Congress, but in many traditional Republican strongholds in state and local government, including in Texas.

The S&P 500 SPX and the Nasdaq Composite COMP both saw a record wipeout in market value on Thursday, but rose to recover some of those losses Friday.

"It won't change the overall endgame - just the pace will likely slow a bit," Oliver Chambers, a senior portfolio manager at Clark Capital, said Friday about AI debt supply and the election results.

Debt financing - now the lifeblood of the AI buildout -could start at a more moderate pace in the first quarter of 2027, as Wall Street tries to figure out "the rules of the road" under the new political landscape, Chambers said.

He isn't expecting the endgame to change in terms of the total number of data centers, but only potentially delay the pace of construction and spending, which could give tech giants' revenues some time to "catch up and expand."

Chambers said recent "pro-business" comments from Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojos also were a positive, given the state's large data-center footprint.

Denny Fish, Janus Henderson's head of technology research and a portfolio manager, said in emailed comments Friday that he expects the AI buildout to continue, "but the locations in which it will be concentrated, and the pace of the rollout, are now in question."

Meanwhile, there's also hope that more infrastructure financing will be shouldered outside of the corporate bond market. AI exposure increased to 5.14% of the investment-grade corporate index as of late October, up from 2.73% at the start of 2025, according to BofA Global data. That makes it hard for any bond fund to avoid altogether.

The supply deluge and volatility this year have pressured investment-grade AI corporate bonds, which have been trading at a large premium to the rest of the market. The difference was about 148 basis points above the risk-free Treasury rate on Thursday, versus 77 basis points for the rest of the market, according to BofA Global. (One basis point is 0.01 percentage point.)

That means investors have been demanding more compensation to offset perceived AI risks.

Next year, BofA Global expects AI-related issuance that's funded in credit markets to peak at about $685 billion, rising about 31% from this year. Yet the yearly increase would come almost entirely from private credit, which tends to be unrated, according to BofA's latest estimates.

For bond pickers like Chambers, 2026 has been all about investors drinking from a fire hose of supply as the hyperscalers have raced to borrow - but the path ahead looks to be more about differentiating the winners and losers of AI, he said.

Related: Nvidia, AMD and other chip stocks rebound. Is the 'violent' AI selloff over?

-Joy Wiltermuth

data.title: Top News Today/Canada: Unemployment Rate Climbs to Six-Month High
data.description:
HEADLINES

Unemployment Rate Climbs to Six-Month High of 6.7%

Canada's labor market weakened for a third straight month in October, with the jobless rate climbing to a six-month high as employment slipped and more people hunted for work.

The economy lost a net 4,700 jobs in October and the unemployment rate rose for a second month in a row, advancing 0.2 percentage point to 6.7%, Statistics Canada said Friday.

The modest pullback in employment builds on the 110,000 jobs lost over the previous two months and unwinds a summer recovery. While the unemployment rate remains below the recent peak of 6.9% in April, employment has now fallen by 45,900 in 2026, adding to signs Canada's economy has lost steam and raising further questions about how much further interest rates might rise in response to inflation risk.

Democrats Are Hatching a Plan to Reverse Trump's Canada Tariffs

Democrats are eyeing President Trump's trade war with Canada as the first target in a campaign to roll back his administration's tariff agenda, according to the party's senior trade lawmaker in the Senate.

"There is overwhelming support for repealing the tariffs on products from Canada," said Sen. Ron Wyden (D., Ore.), the Ranking Member on the Senate Finance Committee, who added that he was "already talking" with colleagues about legislation to push against Trump's second-term levies after he gains control of the committee in January.

Wyden's statement follows an election season when many victorious Democratic candidates called for an end to Trump's trade conflict with Canada, which threatens to intensify in the coming months before the new lawmakers are sworn in.

Carney Eyes Expanding Breadth of Trade With China

Brookfield Asset Management Fundraises $25 Billion in Quarter, Led by Infrastructure Strategies

Brookfield Asset Management is seeing no let up in fundraising efforts as it tracks toward a record year, driven by the alternative asset manager's infrastructure franchise as investors seek out real assets for stability and returns.

The firm said it fundraised $25 billion in the just-ended quarter, bringing the year-to-date total to $123 billion.

"Our fundraising is showing no signs of slowing down," Chief Executive Connor Teskey said.

Enbridge Third-Quarter Profit Rises on Derivative Gains

Enbridge reported higher third-quarter profit, supported by steady distributable cash flow growth and noncash gains on financial hedging contracts.

The energy-infrastructure company posted a rise in net income to C$1.29 billion, or C$0.59 a share, up from C$682 million, or C$0.30 a share, in the comparable quarter a year earlier.

Enbridge noted that the increase was largely due to noncash, unrealized gains in the fair value of derivative instruments used to hedge foreign exchange, interest rates and commodity prices.

Telus Logs Third-Quarter Loss on Writedowns, Revenue Falls

Telus swung to a third-quarter loss after recording a large goodwill impairment tied to its divestiture plans, while revenue also declined.

Shares fell 2.9% to C$12.81.

The telecom company swung to a loss of C$660 million, or C$0.42 a share, compared with a profit of C$431 million, or C$0.32 a share, in the comparable quarter a year ago.

The decline was due to a C$800 million noncash writedown at its Telus Health segment due to lowered growth expectations, weak market conditions, and valuation marks tied to the company's active divestiture process.

Saputo Beats Views on Growing Demand for High-Protein Dairy Products

Saputo shares rose after a surge in demand for high-protein dairy ingredients helped the company offset higher input costs and a soft cheese market in its fiscal second quarter.

Shares rose 5.7% to C$43.99.

The Montreal-based dairy processor reported 3.6% growth in revenue to C$4.26 billion, edging past forecasts, with adjusted earnings of C$0.55 a share coming in 6 cents ahead of consensus expectations.

Emera Profit Drops, Unveils C$21.5 Billion Capital Plan

Emera logged lower third-quarter profit, raised its dividend and unveiled an expanded five-year capital plan aimed at Florida's growing energy demand.

The Halifax, Nova Scotia-based energy services company posted a decline in net income to C$182 million, or C$0.59 a share, down from C$228 million, or C$0.76 a share, in the comparable quarter a year ago. The company noted that earnings were weighed down by a C$41 million after-tax mark-to-market loss and merger transaction costs.

Emera is launching a C$21.5 billion capital plan which is forecast to drive a rate-base growth of between 7.5% and 8.5% through 2030, an increase from a previous range of between 7% and 8%.

Canadian Utilities Third-Quarter Profit Falls on Higher Costs

Canadian Utilities reported lower third-quarter profit due to legal and legislative charges in the period.

The Calgary, Alberta-based utility company posted net income of C$94 million, or C$0.28 a share, down from C$100 million, or C$0.29 a share, in the comparable quarter a year ago.

The decline was due largely to C$87 million in combined after-tax charges, including a C$56 million impact from an Alberta Court of Appeal ruling upholding non-recoverable customer rate refunds, and a C$31 million post-employment benefit obligation adjustment stemming from healthcare legislation in the province.

Algonquin Power Logs Lower Profit on Higher Costs

Cineplex Profit, Revenue Jump as Moviegoers Rush to the Big Screens

Cineplex reported a surge in third-quarter profit and revenue, propelled by an influx of moviegoers lining up for such blockbusters as Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey.

The Canadian movie theater chain posted net income of C$23.8 million, or C$0.34 a share, up from C$1.2 million, or C$0.02 a share, in the comparable quarter a year ago. According to FactSet, analysts were expecting C$0.42 a share.

Total revenues rose by 26% to C$440.2 million, comfortably ahead of analyst forecasts expecting a more modest rise to C$423 million.

IMAX Has a Record Quarter

TALKING POINT

Bank of Canada to Maintain 2% Inflation Target in Renewed Framework

By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--The Bank of Canada and the country's finance department agreed Thursday to renew the central bank's inflation-targeting framework for another five years, with an emphasis on keeping headline inflation at 2%.

The central bank was among the first to adopt an inflation-targeting regime in the early 1990s, with a goal to set interest rates to achieve and maintain 2% inflation. According to a joint statement, the government and central bank said the 12-month change in the consumer-price index would act as the beacon for policymakers.

"The experience of the past five years has reinforced the value of a clear and credible inflation-targeting framework that provides the bank with the mandate and the flexibility to respond decisively to changing economic conditions," the central bank and finance department said in the statement.

Further details will be forthcoming in a speech that Bank of Canada Gov. Tiff Macklem is scheduled to deliver Nov. 24 in Toronto.

Unlike the renewal in 2021, references to securing maximum employment were absent in the joint statement. The Federal Reserve has a dual mandate of achieving low, stable inflation and maximum employment through rate policy.

"I think it's interesting that there's less emphasis on employment and on core inflation in favor of more emphasis on headline inflation," BMO Capital Markets' economist Shelly Kaushik said after reviewing the joint statement. "I think more focus on headline inflation certainly reads as more hawkish over the short term."

In a speech last year, Macklem said officials had no intention of modifying the 2% target. Instead, he said, officials were reviewing whether policymakers have the right gauges of core inflation in place, and whether shelter costs are distorting certain inflation readings.

The latest CPI report for Canada indicated that prices rose 3.1% in September from a year ago, while indicators of core inflation--which strips out energy and food prices--remained stable and close to 2%. The Bank of Canada late last month raised its policy rate by a quarter point, to 2.5%, on the expectation that total inflation will remain above 3% until late next year.

Economists like David Rosenberg of Rosenberg Research have argued that rate hikes might not be necessary given readings of core CPI, which are meant to focus on underlying price movements by stripping out volatile items.

The Bank of Canada faced criticism earlier this decade when inflation ramped up to historically high levels shortly after the peak of the Covid-19 pandemic, forcing Macklem and senior officials to aggressively raise rates, sparking a slowdown in economic activity.

The central bank said it thoroughly reviewed that period "and harvested lessons" about setting rate policy. "The bank views the episode not as a failure of the framework's design, but as a challenge to its implementation amid extraordinary global shocks," the joint statement said.
